svg.title: Four places the money goes, drawn deliberately equal
svg.desc: A banner across the top says all four cards below are the same width on purpose, that the ordering of the levers is the claim and the sizes are not. Beneath it an arrow runs the width of the canvas, from the host end where the model reads, out past your server. Four equal cards sit along it. The first two are marked host side and both concern model tokens: tool descriptions, driven by the whole catalog being sent to the model on every turn whether it is used or not, whose levers are shorter descriptions, fewer published tools, and a stable order so prompt caching can hit; and tool results, billed at the size you returned and billed again on every later turn they stay in context, whose levers are summarizing on the server and returning a resource link rather than the whole blob. The third card is marked your side: your compute, driven mostly by waiting on someone else's network rather than by processing anything, whose levers are sizing for concurrency, setting a memory limit, and preferring many small replicas to one large one, and which is noted as usually the smallest line. The fourth is marked beyond you: backend and egress, driven by the queries your tools make and the bytes leaving your network, whose levers are ttlMs and cacheScope on the six cacheable methods, and pagination rather than dumping. A panel at the foot says the only ranking that is true is the one you measured, that the way to get it is to put the token counts the host already reports next to the span durations from the trace, and that one day of that beats any figure quoted from somebody else's deployment. A closing line says a number without a workload attached to it is not a number.
svg.text: Where the money goes, and which lever is actually yours
Four cards, one width. Not to scale, and no proportions are claimed.
All four cards are the same width on purpose. The ordering of the levers is the claim; the sizes are not.
at the host, where the model reads
The only ranking that is true is the one you measured
Take the token counts your host already reports and put them next to the span durations from the trace in section 7.
One day of that beats any figure quoted from somebody else's deployment, including this one.
A number without a workload attached to it is not a number.
